messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am evaluating the current distribution and habitat selection, and assessing the extent of any declines in occupancy at historical sites of an endemic chipmunk in the package unmarked. I surveyed 160 random sites stratified across 4 landcover types, and 55 non-random sites (resurveyed 50 historical sites and 5 sites in a recent burned area). There was about 42 random sites occupied, 15 historical sites occupied, and all 5 burned sites were occupied.

To evaluate the current distribution and habitat selection, I am considering combining all the data I have collected (random and non-random sites). Is there any literature that discusses the validity of using non-random data, or utilizes and acknowledges their use of non-random sites?

If I were to combine the random and non-random sites, one potential path could be creating a random vs non-random/historical covariate. I would then test that covariate as a detection and occupancy covariate to see if non-random/historical sites influenced detection and/or occupancy probability.

Thank you for your help in advance!

Hailey

messages.subject_clean: Stacked years: single season or N-mixture?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Natalia,

I'm far less knowledgeable than many on this forum, but I think you're right that if data from each year were from different sites, you would not be able to separate the differences in year from the differences in site.  So, you might still be able to stack the data and get an estimate of overall occupancy, but with confounded variables (site and year) you wouldn't know what is causing any differences.  If you did stack them, you would need to include a covariate to represent the site/year, knowing this variable is confounded but perhaps helpful in getting overall estimates.  I think, particularly with scarce data, you would have to have some repeated measures in your data (within each site/year) in order for the models to run.  Either way, you'd need to be sure not to violate the assumption of closure.

To Juan's original post, N-mixture models estimate abundance.  To estimate presence, you need to use an occupancy model.  Further, in my experience N-mix models need more data to converge than occupancy models, so with sparse detections, occupancy models are probably a safer bet.

-Alex

Are the estimates more reasonable values when you fit the null model? I'd suggest fitting models iteratively, making them progressively more complex until you can identify which covariate(s) might be causing the problem.

Ken

messages.subject: Re: Stacked years: single season or N-mixture?
messages.subject_clean: Stacked years: single season or N-mixture?
messages.body_plain:
Juan and Natalia,

You can stack your data since you are not worried about yearly turnover rates. It does not matter that you surveyed different sites in different years when you are strictly investigating habitat variables associated with occupancy. This topic is covered in the McKenzie et al. book (Occupancy Estimation and Modeling Inferring Patterns and Dynamics of Species Occurrence).

Juan,

Since you are using camera trap data I highly recommend the Royle and Nichols 2003 model (Royle, J. A., & Nichols, J. D. (2003). Estimating abundance from repeated presence–absence data or point counts. Ecology, 84(3), 777-790.) since the model accounts for unmodeled heterogeneity in detection among sites. Which is extremely common in camera trap data. The model does produce an abundance estimate; however, you can convert it to psi. The function in unmark to convert the estimate is lambda2psi.

As for model implementation I would recommend choosing the number of surveys that you feel is appropriate (possibly the max number of surveys conducted over the 10 years) and fill in NAs for any missing data like you would for nonstacked data. Each site would then have its own covariates that are associated with it in the SiteCovs of the unmarked frame.  Since the surveys were taken at different times over a long survey period I would recommend modeling a Julian date  covariate in your detection model.

-Ryan

On Wednesday, March 9, 2022 at 1:37:57 PM UTC-8 aw...@scenichudson.org wrote:
> Hi Natalia,
>
> I'm far less knowledgeable than many on this forum, but I think you're right that if data from each year were from different sites, you would not be able to separate the differences in year from the differences in site.  So, you might still be able to stack the data and get an estimate of overall occupancy, but with confounded variables (site and year) you wouldn't know what is causing any differences.  If you did stack them, you would need to include a covariate to represent the site/year, knowing this variable is confounded but perhaps helpful in getting overall estimates.  I think, particularly with scarce data, you would have to have some repeated measures in your data (within each site/year) in order for the models to run.  Either way, you'd need to be sure not to violate the assumption of closure.
>
> To Juan's original post, N-mixture models estimate abundance.  To estimate presence, you need to use an occupancy model.  Further, in my experience N-mix models need more data to converge than occupancy models, so with sparse detections, occupancy models are probably a safer bet.
>

messages.subject: distsampOpen and time trends
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am a master's student using open-population distance sampling models to assess changes in bird abundance over a breeding season.

I am comparing bird abundances in crop sites and native sites and trying to see if they change differentially between site types over the breeding season. (My hypothesis is that abundance declines on crop sites as the season progresses and increases on native sites.)

I used distance sampling methods in the field to obtain bird counts:
2 summers (2020-2021)
6 survey rounds each year (May - July)
50 survey plots each year, 100 total.

I was going to pool all data and use year as a covariate, but due to one drought year I plan to run the analysis separately for each year to show these differences between year more directly. Anyway, I was excited to see that the distsampOpen function was developed and I plan on using it to assess trends in bird abundance over the breeding season. Having 6 rounds of distance sampling surveys each year should allow me to do this.

I am a little confused on which dynamics parameterization to use. I have used "trend" and modeled effects of covariates on detection, effects of site type (crop or native) on initial abundance, and the effect of scaled Julian date on gamma. I don't know if it would be better to use time as a factor covariate (survey rounds 1-6). I know it would be more parsimonious to use Julian date, so I was hoping someone could provide some insight and help explain the difference to me. Also, if I just want to model a time trend, am I overcomplicating things by using this type of model?

Alternatively, I could use "constant" and model effects of site type and time (date) on initial abundance, survival, and recruitment. In this case I would assume site type may influence initial abundance and date may influence gamma and or omega. If I use "constant", this means changes in abundance are the result of a Markov process--is this also the case if I use "trend"? Sorry for my limited understanding, but there isn't as much help out there for this model type as for others.

Thank you,

Amber

I am working with unmarked and am having trouble with the predicted occupancy values, particularly finding the standard error of the mean using the delta method.

What is the best way to go about this?

###############################################################
#top model
occ_modgame = occu(~ Temp + Wave_adj ~ Location + PH_indicator, gamebird.occ)

messages.body_plain:
That paper has the following:  "...investigators might consider using 85% confidence intervals so that model-selection and parameter-evaluation criteria are more congruent."

So if one lives and dies by AIC (and have read Arnold's paper), then maybe 85% is the way to go.  (Although if I understood the paper correctly,the congruence is about the 2 AIC units rule more closely matching conclusions with 85% confidence intervals.  If so, why not keep 95% and change the AIC rule?)

But if one has not taken into consideration the consequences/costs of either making a right or wrong decision, then I would stick with 95% as it is a common standard despite it being arbitrary.  Certainly in the past folks have used 80% (and 50%) because the smaller intervals give the appearance of more precision.  The best way to cause confusion is to use a variety of standards.  (In the distant past I've seen folks who go the other direction and want 99% confidence intervals to justify that their chemical processes were in control - their confidence intervals were so wide that it became nearly impossible to declare a process was out of whack.  And yet they claimed "More confidence!!" in their results.)

Jim

Hi Jaran,

If you choose modavgPred( , type = "response"), the confidence
intervals presented for the predictions are first computed on the logit
scale and then the limits are back-transformed on the probability scale
so that they remain within the [0, 1] interval. They are not computed
on the probability scale and this explains the discrepancy. I also note
that some of the predictions you report are on the boundary which can
make it harder to get reliable SE's and CI's.

You can send me the data and models saved as an R file offlist if you
want so I can check if anything else is going on.
